title: Article Can You Recover From an AI-Era Attack?
summary: Prepare for an AI-era attack by strengthening cyber resilience, testing recovery plans, and protecting the data your business needs to operate.
body_markdown:
## **Key takeaways**


- AI can compress the time defenders have to detect, contain, and respond to an attack.
- Backups alone do not prove that critical applications and business services can be recovered.
- Recovery planning should prioritize business impact, validated recovery targets, and protected recovery environments.
- AI readiness depends on trusted, available data, making data protection and resilience part of the AI foundation.


### Cyber resilience starts with recovery readiness.


Most organizations believe they’re prepared for a cyberattack. They have backups. They’ve invested in security tools. They’ve documented recovery plans.


According to John Valentine, senior manager of services at Insight, that is often where the problem begins.


“Most teams assume they’re protected


, but they’ve never tested whether recovery would actually hold up


.”
John Valentine, Insight


As AI accelerates how attackers identify vulnerabilities, automate reconnaissance, and move through environments, you have less time to react. Yet Valentine believes many businesses are focused on the wrong question. The challenge is not simply preventing an attack. It’s recovering from one.


## AI is changing the recovery conversation.


AI is transforming how you operate. It is also changing the pace of cyberthreats.


According to Valentine, security teams face an environment where the window between exposure and exploitation continues to shrink. Mandiant’s M-Trends 2026 now estimates mean time to exploit at negative seven days — down from 63 days in 2018 — meaning exploitation frequently begins before a patch exists.¹ CrowdStrike’s 2026 Global Threat Report found average eCrime breakout time fell to 29 minutes in 2025, a 65% increase in speed year over year.²


But Valentine cautions against viewing this solely as a security problem. Recovery deserves equal attention.


“If a critical system went down right now, how long would it take you to recover?”


For many businesses, the answer is not nearly as clear as leadership believes. Most resilience strategies have historically focused on prevention and protection. Far fewer teams have invested the same effort in proving recovery will work when it matters most.


### **“Backups are now the perfect target.”**


According to John Valentine, many organizations still think of backups as a last line of defense.


The problem is that sophisticated attackers understand that, too.


Backups are often targeted before the main disruption becomes visible. By the time ransomware is deployed or systems are encrypted, attackers may have already spent days or weeks compromising recovery infrastructure, deleting backup copies, corrupting data, or disabling the tools needed for restoration.


That’s what makes recoverability different from backup.


You might have data copies.


But if those copies can’t be trusted, can’t be accessed, or can’t restore the business in the time required, then the backup strategy has already failed.


## Downtime reaches beyond IT.


When cyber incidents are discussed, the conversation often focuses on technology. Valentine believes that view is too narrow. The real question is what happens to your business when critical systems become unavailable.


Consider a retailer losing access to point-of-sale systems. They wouldn’t just lose their POS technology; they’d lose most of their efficiency tools. Transactions would stop. Inventory visibility would disappear. Employees would have to shift to manual workarounds that cannot support normal operations.


The technology outage is only the beginning. Every hour spent restoring services can affect productivity, client experiences, revenue, and trust. Recovery discussions need to connect directly to business outcomes. The question isn’t whether a server can be restored. It’s whether the business can function.


## Can you prove recoverability?


Many teams measure backup success. Few measure recoverability. For Valentine, that’s one of the most important distinctions leaders need to understand.


“Can we actually recover in the event of an attack?”


This question can reveal gaps that routine backup reports never uncover. Recovery plans may exist on paper but have never been tested. Critical application dependencies may not be documented. Failover procedures may rely on manual processes. Recovery targets may be assumptions rather than proven capabilities.


Recoverability replaces those assumptions with evidence. This requires you to understand:


### Which applications are most critical to the business.


### How long recovery will take.


### How much data loss is acceptable.


### Whether current recovery procedures work.


Without that validation, your recovery posture may rest on hope rather than proof.


## Why recovery becomes harder after an attack.


One of Valentine’s most compelling observations is that recovery challenges do not necessarily end when an attack is contained. In some cases, they are just beginning.


He points to businesses that have struggled for months to restore normal operations after a significant cyber event. Even when encrypted systems can technically be unlocked, recovery is rarely as simple as pressing a button.


“They give you the keys. They don’t tell you how to use them.”


Teams may still need to rebuild environments, validate data integrity, re-establish application dependencies, verify system configurations, and determine which assets remain trustworthy. Those efforts take time. They also reinforce a critical point: A recovery strategy should not begin during a recovery event.


## Build resilience before the crisis.


Valentine recommends starting with the applications and services that have the greatest impact on daily operations. Not everything needs to be recovered at once. The goal is to understand what matters most and prioritize recovery accordingly.


From there, validate recoverability through testing, business impact analysis, and recovery assessments.


Ask:


- Which systems are most critical to operations?
- How long could those systems remain unavailable?
- Have recovery procedures been tested recently?
- Are recovery targets realistic?


The answers create a clearer picture of resilience than a backup report alone can provide.


## Prove you can recover.


Cybersecurity remains essential. Prevention remains critical. But when attacks continue to evolve and accelerate, resilience cannot be treated as an afterthought.


Valentine’s message is straightforward: Stop assuming recovery will work. Prove it.


When a serious outage occurs, leaders will not ask how many backup jobs completed successfully. Employees and clients will care about how quickly the business returns to normal.


In the AI era, resilience isn’t a line in a backup report — it’s a business guarantee. The organizations that treat recovery as a rehearsed discipline, not an assumption, will be the ones still standing when the next AI-accelerated attack hits. The rest will find out how prepared they really are in the worst possible moment.


“Don’t just store your data. Make sure you can get it back.”
